headline: High-risk shared-workspace pair: LangGraph can feed Replit Agent unverified state, creating dangerous default paths for leakage, conflicts, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph is a library with application-defined files and shared checkpointer state, so attacker-controlled content can reach Replit Agent through the workspace or persisted graph state. Replit Agent reads and writes Repl workspace files by default. This is not provably a manual-only bridge, so the interaction pathway exists in default-ish deployments.
conditions: IF LangGraph nodes persist untrusted text into the checkpointer or workspace files, THEN Replit Agent may ingest it as instructions.
IF the two agents share a Repl workspace or synced file path, THEN prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces or containers.
Mark all cross-agent files as data-only and strip instructions before handoff.
Add a human review step before Replit Agent reads LangGraph outputs.
Use allowlisted schemas for any shared state.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every shared artifact.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph can touch graph state and model-provider API keys, while Replit Agent touches source code, secrets, and deployment configuration. Replit Agent also has broad network egress and file access. If they share workspace state, sensitive code or secrets can flow from A into B and then out through B's networked tools, making leakage plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF LangGraph stores secrets or sensitive graph state in shared files, THEN Replit Agent can read them.
IF Replit Agent sends workspace contents to external APIs or package registries, THEN those secrets can leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspace files.
Use separate secret stores for each agent.
Disable network access for the Replit Agent during shared-state handling.
Redact sensitive fields before passing outputs across agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and broad network egress. LangGraph can persist shared state via a checkpointer store, while Replit Agent persists filesystem state across sessions. Concurrent writes to the same workspace or state store can corrupt files, overwrite code, or race on deployment artifacts without built-in locking.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or checkpointer-backed state, THEN race conditions can corrupt artifacts.
IF either agent modifies deployment or build files concurrently, THEN one agent can overwrite the other's changes.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory.
Serialize writes with a lock file or queue.
Freeze deployment files while the other agent is active.
Use git branches or snapshots for handoff.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is explicitly a graph of nodes where each node may itself be an agent, so its outputs are likely to be treated as structured upstream state. Replit Agent acts on workspace files and deployment configuration. If Replit consumes LangGraph output without verification, a mistaken plan or hallucinated fact can cascade into code changes or deployment actions.
conditions: IF Replit Agent reads LangGraph-produced files as authoritative, THEN unverified content can drive actions.
IF LangGraph emits incorrect structured state that Replit Agent converts into code or deployment edits, THEN the error cascades downstream.
mitigations: Require explicit validation before Replit Agent acts on LangGraph output.
Add schema checks for every handoff file.
Keep a human approval gate before code or deployment changes.
Log and diff all upstream outputs before execution.
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts between the agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Replit Agent explicitly handles source code, secrets, and deployment configuration in a Repl-managed cloud container, while LangGraph handles graph state and model-provider keys. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of sensitive data.
conditions: IF regulated data such as secrets or customer code is placed into the shared workflow, THEN residency or retention obligations may apply.
IF the deployment environment requires specific retention or deletion guarantees, THEN the pair may violate them unless configured.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared agent workflows.
Review retention settings for both platforms.
Use separate environments for regulated and non-regulated work.
Document data flow and residency before deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
